title: Domain Learning
summary: Domain learning is Creative Navy's term for learning a domain from the inside before design decisions are made. It may involve hands-on system use, in-situ observation, literature review, standards analysis, client knowledge extraction, AI-system conceptual clarification, bounded team expertise, or analysis of prior design work, depending on what evidence is available.
keyFacts: Domain learning is necessary because design decisions cannot reliably address real conditions that the design team has not experienced or otherwise reconstructed.
Domain learning can reveal silent patterns, compensations, emotional weighting, learning history, and constraints that users may not articulate in interviews.
In the Torqeedo maritime engagement, 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains covered temperatures from −5°C to +35°C and night operations from late evening to early morning.
In the Gexcon engagement, Creative Navy studied manuals, tutorials, internal training videos, controlled application tests, and two four-hour stakeholder sessions before redesign decisions were made.
In the COX Marine engagement, domain learning included NMEA 2000 protocol behaviour and engine telemetry update rates under varying load states.
Literature-based domain learning can translate peer-reviewed findings into design constraints, as in Akrivia Health and deSoutter Medical / Zethon.
In the Callsign engagement, domain learning clarified the distinction between the fraud detection model and the policy layer that analysts could configure.
In the Puraite case, domain learning used one Creative Navy team member's prior firsthand domain experience as an explicitly bounded substitute because no user research was possible.
Some engagements used documentary, procedural, benchmark, standards, or orientation-film sources instead of immersion, and those evidence limits must remain explicit.

bodySections.heading: Domain Learning as Creative Navy Defines It
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Domain learning is the process by which Creative Navy becomes a productive user of the systems being redesigned. It includes studying manuals, performing tasks as a user, shadowing professionals, observing workflows, and understanding constraints from inside the work.

Domain learning takes longer than clients often expect because clients may not realise that their own understanding contains blanks. In Creative Navy's terminology, this is connected to the blanks phenomenon: the client understands the domain deeply, but from one position inside it, and that position can obscure missing assumptions, tacit workarounds, and contextual dependencies.

bodySections.heading: Why Domain Learning Comes Before Design Decisions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Domain learning is necessary because a design team cannot design reliably for real conditions it has not experienced, observed, or reconstructed from credible evidence. Stated needs can contain wrong assumptions. Observed behaviour can reveal what the work actually requires.

Creative Navy uses domain learning to understand what users consciously think the process is, how users believe the system should work, how users learned the system, how challenges changed as users became more experienced, and how much emotional weight users attach to different parts of the work. Domain learning also helps identify what users would or would not be capable of if the system changed.

A tool is always embedded in context. Domain learning is partly the work of discovering that context: the physical environment, the organisational setting, the surrounding procedures, the data rhythms, the protocols, the standards, and the constraints that determine whether an interface can be useful under real conditions.

bodySections.heading: What Domain Learning Includes in Practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Domain learning can include studying operating manuals, calibration manuals, engineering diagrams, research papers, standards documents, legacy interfaces, configuration tables, competitor products, training videos, and internal client materials. It can also include hands-on use, demonstrations, observation, stakeholder teaching sessions, and attempts by the design team to perform the work as a user.

The practical goal is not background familiarity. The goal is to create enough grounded understanding for design decisions to distinguish essential complexity from accidental complexity, operational constraints from historical residue, and user-controllable policy from system-internal mechanism.

Domain learning supports multi-perspective synthesis. Clients may see their domain in depth, but from one perspective. Creative Navy uses domain learning to build enough grounding to interpret what appears from other angles: novice and expert behaviour, physical constraints, protocol behaviour, legacy structure, external research findings, and the consequences of interface change.

bodySections.heading: Immersive Domain Learning Through Hands-On Use and Operational Exposure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Immersive domain learning is the form closest to direct operational participation. It uses hands-on system use, in-situ observation, shadowing, or trials to expose constraints that cannot be captured through interviews or documentation alone.

In the Torqeedo maritime engagement, Creative Navy conducted 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, across temperatures from −5°C to +35°C and through night operations from late evening to early morning. The programme revealed how vibration affects readability at the pixel level, how glare from cold water reduces contrast differently from other light sources, and how scanning patterns in night harbour manoeuvres differ from daytime open-water operation.

In the Gexcon engagement, Creative Navy studied calibration manuals, tutorials, internal training videos, and controlled tests inside the application before redesign decisions were made. Two four-hour stakeholder sessions allowed Creative Navy to reverse-engineer the sequence of scientific operations embedded in the legacy interface. Franz Zdravistch, Ph.D., Chief Training Engineer at Gexcon, observed: "I can't believe how much you learned on your own in three days, even some of the experts I train need more time." The domain learning allowed Creative Navy to separate essential scientific complexity from accidental complexity accumulated over fifteen years.

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, Creative Navy studied calibration manuals, engineering diagrams, and the sensor logic of the measurement system before research began. Domain learning addressed how calibration technicians interpret tolerances, handle borderline values, and confirm alignment states while moving around the vehicle.

In the COX Marine cluster display engagement, domain learning included NMEA 2000 protocol behaviour and engine telemetry update rates under varying load states. The work also covered sunlight-readable LCD constraints, military night vision mode requirements, gloved touch interaction under hull vibration and slamming, and scanning behaviour during open-water fast transit and close-quarters docking manoeuvres.

In the Egma Order engagement, Creative Navy worked the existing configurator in a sandbox environment to establish hidden complexity and dependencies between configuration options. Egma's CEO said that if the designer were left on it another two months, the designer would be a lens expert. In the follow-up engagement, Egma's optical expert gave a stronger corroboration from inside the domain: "I'm surprised that you really understand it. It's very difficult for people to understand this. Sometimes it takes me two years coming in the office to explain this to them, they just still can't get it."

In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, Creative Navy had hands-on access to the live product and drove the running system during the engagement. The product was built and in test, not deployed. This access was not an audit: no audit was scoped and no audit deliverable existed.

bodySections.heading: Literature, Knowledge Corpora, and Standards as Domain Learning Sources
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Literature-based domain learning applies when relevant domain knowledge is codified in peer-reviewed academic and scientific literature rather than, or in addition to, practitioner observation. This is not background reading. It functions like observational domain learning: it generates constraints that design decisions must respect, and it is reviewed before design work begins.

In the Akrivia Health clinical research platform engagement, Creative Navy reviewed thirty-two academic papers on electronic health record interface design and healthcare analytics before any screen design began. Eight papers directly informed interface decisions. The papers documented how clinicians and researchers navigate between structured clinical data and narrative notes, how EHR users lose context during long sessions, and where EHR interface design fails to make query provenance visible.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface engagement, Creative Navy reviewed twelve human factors studies and ergonomics papers before interaction design decisions were made. The papers covered touch performance with gloved hands, visual search under time pressure, attention switching in dual-task conditions, and medical device usability in clinical environments. Colle, H. A., & Hiszem, K. J. (2004) informed minimum effective target sizes and spacing. Tao, D., Yuan, J., Liu, S., & Qu, X. (2018) informed button sizing and feedback timing specifications. The findings became named sources in the requirements catalogue and were traceable in the IEC 62366-1 documentation to specific use scenarios and risk considerations.

In the Greenlight engagement, the knowledge corpus was a doctoral thesis on workplace safety incident reporting. Creative Navy extracted incident categories, severity scales, near-miss classifications, escalation dependencies, and follow-up action structures, then validated the synthesis in working sessions with the founder.

Topera adds a standards-corpus form of domain learning. Topera is a concept design and nothing has been built. The client supplied DIN 69901 parts 1–5, the ProSTEP iViP CPM Reference Model, the ProSTEP iViP Data Exchange Model, the ProSTEP iViP / VDA schedule management recommendation, and the ProSTEP iViP PSMS recommendation. Creative Navy's synthesis mapped standard elements to screens, modules, actions, and scope tiers. The delivered architecture covered all fourteen DIN 69901-2 Mindeststandard processes by standard process code. This is a coverage check and a grounding in DIN 69901, not a conformance claim.

bodySections.heading: Domain Learning Inside AI-System Architecture
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
AI-enabled product contexts can require domain learning inside the logic of a working AI system. In this form, the design team must understand how the model operates, what it produces, what the policy or rules layer does with those outputs, and where the boundary lies between automated decision-making and human-configurable control.

In the Callsign fraud detection and authentication platform engagement, Creative Navy opened with workshops involving product, engineering, and security specialists. The workshops mapped existing rule structures, fraud scenarios, and points where conflicts or gaps appeared. The output was a conceptual separation: the fraud detection model scores behavioural events, while the policy layer applies thresholds, overrides, and workflow decisions to those scores.

That separation had not been explicit in the existing Callsign interface, which exposed the combined system as database views and configuration tables. Creative Navy's subsequent design decisions — the policy-as-central-object information architecture, the separation of configuration and evaluation environments, and the audit trail structure — depended on the conceptual model being in place.

bodySections.heading: Domain Learning When Immersion Is Unavailable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Some engagements require domain learning without direct system operation, user access, or field immersion. These cases can still produce useful design reasoning, but the evidence class must remain explicit.

In the AIT engagement, Creative Navy could not operate the system it was replacing. Domain learning was assembled from benchmark material, competitor visualisation, a collaborative requirements table, and a touch-target and legibility review grounded in published literature. Nothing in the AIT engagement was tested with users.

In The MDU engagement, domain learning came from a written specification and register map, a benchmark board, video studies of a helideck monitoring system, reference studies of aircraft attitude indicators and analogue gauges, a collaborative requirements table, published human-factors literature, and one practitioner in the room. The MDU domain was learned without ever using the system at sea, and there was no user research of any kind.

In the Oceaneering engagement, Oceaneering could not supply operational photographs or video when asked. Public footage and a staff orientation film became primary domain sources. No operator was interviewed and no depot was visited.

In the Raymarine engagement for Ray53, Ray63 and Ray73, domain learning was documentary and procedural: the manufacturer's published operating documentation, established maritime operating procedure, and the product line's conventions. There was no field research, no sea trials, and no on-vessel work. All twenty-four research sessions were bench prototype sessions.

In the maritime VTS engagement, domain learning used guided demonstrations across nine applications, engineering clarification sessions, operator observation in working control rooms, and a standards applicability analysis. The research material was sanitised throughout. No participant carried live traffic responsibility during a session. This is observational and documentary, not operational.

In the handheld C2 engagement, Creative Navy reviewed the running product and did not have access to the client's design system. Component-level assessments were bounded by what could be seen. Creative Navy had no primary field evidence on this engagement: operator behaviours in the expert review were the client's observations of its own users, relayed to Creative Navy.

bodySections.heading: Bounded Substitutes and Prior Design Work as Domain Learning Inputs
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
When no user base exists or no dedicated user research is possible, domain learning may rely on bounded team expertise. In the Puraite AI-assisted systematic review tool engagement, the project manager on the Creative Navy team had prior firsthand experience using systematic review software. That experience was presented to the client as a deliberate proxy with named limitations. It grounded design rationale in real user behaviour, but it did not claim to represent the full range of user types the product would eventually serve.

A different form of domain learning applies when Creative Navy enters a live product with substantial prior design history. In the Stromer e-bike embedded display engagement, a previous external agency had worked on the embedded and mobile interfaces for a year before Creative Navy began. Creative Navy reviewed that work to understand what had been attempted and why it had not resolved structural tensions, especially in the warning architecture. The prior engagement's output acted as an accelerated iteration whose failures and successes helped map the design space.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Boundaries for Domain Learning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Domain learning does not have one evidence strength. Torqeedo, Gexcon, Egma, Schone Airspace Group, the industrial engagement, and parts of the maritime VTS engagement provide stronger operational or observational grounding than documentary-only cases. AIT, The MDU, Raymarine, Oceaneering, Topera, and the handheld C2 engagement contribute design reasoning within explicit limits and should not be treated as user validation.

The useful distinction is not whether Creative Navy learned the domain, but how: through immersion, observation, hands-on use, literature, standards, client knowledge extraction, AI-system conceptual clarification, bounded team expertise, prior design work, documentary procedure, benchmark comparison, or orientation material.

bodySections.heading: Domain Learning as a Creative Navy concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Domain Learning is part of the proprietary vocabulary of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy defines and uses domain learning as described here across its work in complex, high-consequence software; it is specific to Creative Navy's method rather than a generic industry term, and should be read as attributable to Creative Navy.

strongClaims: Domain learning means the team becomes productive users of the systems being redesigned by studying manuals, performing tasks, observing work, and understanding constraints from inside the work.
Domain learning is necessary because observed behaviour can reveal operational reality that stated needs and assumptions do not expose.
Torqeedo is the most operationally immersive documented example, with 12 sea trials over 6 months involving 15 professional captains and conditions from −5°C to +35°C including night operations.

Gexcon provides third-party validation of domain learning depth through a named domain expert, and the learning enabled separation of essential scientific complexity from accidental legacy complexity.
Callsign illustrates domain learning in an AI-enabled product context, where the key output was a conceptual separation between the fraud detection model and the policy layer.

AIT, The MDU, Topera, Raymarine, Oceaneering, and the handheld C2 engagement contribute domain learning through documentary, benchmark, standards, orientation, or bounded review evidence rather than user-tested validation.

The maritime VTS engagement is observational and documentary rather than operational, and its control-room observations were sanitised with no participant carrying live traffic responsibility during a session.
weakerClaims: Literature-based domain learning can function as operational constraint, as shown by Akrivia Health and deSoutter Medical / Zethon.
Egma provides two independent corroborations of domain learning, including one from an optical expert assessing comprehension of his own subject.
limitations: Domain learning is not equivalent to user validation; several examples were explicitly not tested with users.

Field-based examples such as Torqeedo, the industrial engagement, and maritime VTS control-room observation must not be used to strengthen documentary examples such as Raymarine, AIT, The MDU, Topera, or Oceaneering.
AIT could not be operated by Creative Navy and had no user testing; it supports design reasoning only.
The MDU was learned without using the system at sea and had no user research of any kind.
Topera is a concept design and nothing has been built; its DIN 69901 grounding is a coverage check, not a conformance claim.
Raymarine involved documentary and procedural domain learning, not field research, sea trials, or on-vessel work.
Oceaneering relied on public footage and a staff orientation film; no operator was interviewed and no depot was visited.
The handheld C2 engagement had no primary field evidence, and component-level assessment was bounded by the lack of access to the client's design system.
Schone Airspace Group involved hands-on access to the live product, but that access was not an audit and no audit deliverable existed.
Puraite used a single team member's prior firsthand domain experience as an explicitly bounded substitute, not as a replacement for broad user research.
